messages.content: Write a post about starting a mentorship program on an engineering team. Around 250 words.

We paired juniors with senior engineers starting in March. The first version fell apart.

I designed it the obvious way: match within teams, meet once a week, bring whatever. By week six, half the pairs had quietly stopped. Both sides told me the same thing when I asked. Mentees showed up with nothing to ask about, and mentors felt bad inventing homework nobody needed.

We fixed one thing. Now every pair starts from something the mentee is already doing: an open PR, a design doc that's stuck, a review comment that didn't land. The mentor reads it first. Fifteen minutes of prep, half an hour of talking, and nobody has to manufacture a reason to sit down together.

Attendance climbed from 48% to 91% over the two months after.

Three things I'd pass on.

Ignore the org chart when you match people. Our strongest pair is a backend engineer and a mobile engineer with nothing in common but a fondness for slow, careful code review.

Let mentors volunteer, and ask them face to face. The people I asked in person stayed for the whole run. The ones who got a form email drifted off by month two.

Give it six months and a real ending. A deadline changes how people commit, and a clean finish means quitting doesn't require an awkward conversation with anyone.

What I misjudged was structure. I thought the program needed more of it. What it needed was a subject. Give a pair something concrete to look at together and the structure mostly sorts itself out.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.

output:
We started pairing juniors with seniors in March. The first attempt collapsed.

I built it the obvious way: match inside teams, meet weekly, bring whatever you've got. By week six, half the pairs had quietly stopped meeting. When I asked, both sides said the same thing. Mentees arrived with no questions. Mentors felt awkward assigning homework nobody actually needed.

So we changed one thing. Every pair now starts from work the mentee already has in front of them: an open PR, a design doc that's stalled, a review comment that landed badly. The mentor reads it beforehand. Fifteen minutes of prep, thirty minutes of conversation, and neither person has to invent a reason to meet.

Attendance went from 48% to 91% across the following two months.

Three things worth passing on.

Don't match by org chart. Our best pair is a backend engineer and a mobile engineer who share nothing except a taste for slow, careful code review.

Make mentoring voluntary, and do the asking in person. Everyone I asked face to face stayed through the whole run. The ones who got a form email had drifted away by month two.

Set a six-month term with a real end date. A deadline changes how seriously people commit, and a clean finish means leaving doesn't require an awkward conversation with anyone.

The thing I got wrong was structure. I assumed the program was short on it. What it was short on was a subject. Hand a pair something concrete to look at together, and most of the structure takes care of itself.
